newsitem.title: JAPAN: US-Japan forex policy difference emerging - experts.
newsitem.headline: US-Japan forex policy difference emerging - experts.

text.p: Washington and Tokyo agree that the recent dollar rally was clearly overdone, but they seem to disagree about how far the dollar should fall against the yen, currency experts say.

"I see Washington wanting the dollar to slide to the point where U.S. manufacturers can manage to compete with powerful Japanese exporters...which is 100-105 yen," said a chief fund manager at an investment management firm in Tokyo.
The dollar has taken a nearly 10 yen dive in just seven trading days from its recent peak and traded as low as 117.50 yen in Tokyo on Monday.

"It is obvious that these American manufacturers are not competitive at all with the dollar at 115 yen, even though Japanese monetary authorities seek a stabilisation of the dollar around 110-120 yen," the manager said.

In an apparent bid to avoid a further nosedive of the U.S. currency, Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Monday that the dollar was likely to settle down soon as the Group of Seven (G7) statement on currencies is digested by the market.
The G7, at a meeting in Washington in late April, emphasised the importance of avoiding exchange rates that could lead to the reemergence of large external imbalances.
But the experts said Japan's signal that the dollar's downward correction may be nearing an end for now is not shared by U.S. monetary authorities.

"The U.S. authorities have not said specifically that they were interested in a stronger yen. However, the market move in that direction would not be opposed by the U.S. Treasury and might even be welcomed," said Robert Feldman, director of Economic Research at Salomon Brothers Asia Ltd.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated on Friday that he shared Japanese concerns about currency movements, though he declined to comment on specific exchange rates.

"Japanese authorities may want to see the dollar stabilise around the 115-120 yen range, a level that would still give (Japanese exporters) a competitive edge," said Takeshi Hanai, executive manager of the Industrial Bank of Japan's International Treasury Department.

But the dollar may slide to around 110 yen or possibly below, given the fact that Japanese institutional investors have yet to hedge against currency losses on their massive non-yen bond exposure and the prospect that Tokyo's surplus will grow massively, IBJ's Hanai said.

Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus for April, due to be announced next Monday, is expected to total 809.9 billion yen ($6.80 billion), up 156.9 percent from 315.3 billion yen ($2.64 billion) a year earlier, private research company Daiwa Bank Research Institute said on Monday.
American industry has admitted the dwindling competitiveness of American goods due to the dollar's rally over the past two years and called for a strong yen.

"As long as the exchange rate is not allowed to appreciate too far, American industry will remain competitive," National Association of Manufacturers (NAM) president Jerry Jasinowski said in late April in testimony to the Senate Commerce subcommittee on manufacturing and competitiveness.
The NAM also said the U.S. trade deficit with Japan indicated the need for a stronger yen.
The NAM said both Washington and Tokyo need to pay more than lip service to the problems caused by a rising dollar.
Analysts said the only quick measure now available for Japan to avoid a swelling external surplus is to strengthen its own currency.

Another option for Japan is drastic deregulation of its economy to create domestic demand for growth. But they said this would take too long to bring about, leaving a stronger yen as the only option for Japan to rein in its surplus. ($1=119 yen)
